## The claim, and what we are doing to it

The original author (OA) studied how citizens frame the European Union. One claim from their paper is our target:

> "… poor economic performances … decrease positive dimensions of EU framing" (Teney 2016: 619)

Operationalised the way that the Multi100 project constrained it for its five analysts: does a country's **unemployment rate** (poor economic performance) lower the **cosmopolitan** dimension of EU framing (peace, democracy, free movement, cultural diversity, a stronger say in the world)? The published result was a coefficient of −0.0034, t = −4.03.

You hold the data, the tools, and the workflow that the project used – and the code you work through is the coordinator's own submitted analysis. You are analyst no. 6, and the question is: how robust is that number to *justifiable* alternative choices? Work through the five tasks below in order, from a setup check to two dots on the live class chart – one explored, one declared.

::: callout-tip
## How the tasks work

Every task is a callout box with instructions, a **TODO** you complete, and code chunks that **already run** – so the report renders from the first preview. You edit the prose blanks and, in Tasks 4 and 5, the code. The browser version of this same exercise is on the course site if you would rather not install anything; this workspace is the full IDE pipeline.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Task 1 – Set up, and fix the vocabulary"}
**First, the setup check.** If this report renders at all, your workspace is working: the packages are installed, the data are in place, and the helpers are loaded. Render it once now, before anything else. If it does not render, run `source("R/check_setup.R")` in the console – it names the packages you are missing and how to install them.

**Then, before touching data, fix the vocabulary.** In the four scenarios below, three are doing one of our three Rs, while one is doing something else entirely.

**TODO: read the four scenarios and fill in the gaps.**

***Scenario 1:*** A reviewer reruns the authors' Stata `.do` file on the authors' data and gets a *different* coefficient from the one printed in the paper. This is an example of \_\_\_\_\_\_, even though what they *tried* to do failed.
***Scenario 2:*** The analyst uses the authors' submitted replication dataset, but they re-implement the model in R instead of Stata and centre the predictor. Is this a case of \_\_\_\_\_\_ or \_\_\_\_\_\_?
***Scenario 3:*** A preregistered team tests the identical hypothesis on a *separate, much larger* dataset chosen to be theoretically equivalent, and gets results that contradict the original. Their conclusion is that the original analysis has failed to \_\_\_\_\_\_.
***Scenario 4:*** Instead of the survey data used by the original authors, another researcher tests the same underlying idea on social-media texts using a machine-learning classifier method that the original never used. To their surprise, the authors' original findings prove \_\_\_\_\_\_ and the researcher concludes that they provide a reliable middle-range theory of the phenomenon they investigate.

*(Answers: 1 reproducibility – the activity is reproducibility even though it failed to match, so the verdict is 'not reproduced'; 2 arguably still reproducibility, a grey area – re-implementing on the same data in different software is a re-computation, though centring the predictor and differing estimator implementations nudge towards robustness; 3 replicability – same question, independent new data; 4 generalisability – the impostor, new data and a new method at once.)*
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Task 2 – Meet the panel"}
The **EU-frames dataset** (`EUframes_cy.csv`) is the country-year panel behind the whole exercise. It is already loaded as `euframes` in the setup chunk, and the copy in `data/` is byte-identical to the one published in the analyst's fork on OSF (osf.io/6zqct – "Multi100 \| Teney_EurSocioRev_2016 \| Analyst_C6HJR", main folder); the official Multi100 archival record is at osf.io/8rtwe.

**TODO:** run the chunks, then read the small-multiples figure. Which countries trend down over 2004–2013? Note one in a comment.

```{r}
#| label: count-data
# How many countries, how many years, how big is the panel?
euframes |>
  summarise(
    countries = n_distinct(cntry),
    years     = n_distinct(year),
    rows      = n()
  )
```

You should see **27 countries**, **10 years** (2004–2013), and **270 rows**. The outcome we care about first is `mcosmo` – the mean cosmopolitan framing of the EU in each country-year (a 0–1 scale). The predictor is `unemp`, the annual unemployment rate; `growth` is annual GDP growth, and `n_cy` counts the survey respondents behind each row. Every column is described in `data/EUframes_cy_codebook.md`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cosmo-trend
#| fig-cap: "Mean cosmopolitan EU framing over time, by country – an echo of OA's Figure 1."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
ggplot(euframes, aes(x = year, y = mcosmo)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey55") +
  geom_point(size = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ cntry, ncol = 6) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2004, 2008, 2013)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean cosmopolitan framing (0–1)")
```

Most countries drift gently; a few move sharply around the 2009 crisis. That variation – within a country, over time – is exactly what the fixed-effects model in Task 3 uses.

*Practising the OSF pull (optional).* `R/get_data.R` fetches this file from the analyst's OSF fork the way that a researcher would, with a course-site mirror as a fallback. It is not needed – the file already ships in `data/` – but running it proves you can pull a real published artefact:

```{r}
#| label: get-data
#| eval: false
# Optional: confirm data/EUframes_cy.csv from OSF (uses the local copy offline).
source("R/get_data.R")
```
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Task 2, continued – name the estimand, draw the graph"}
Before estimating, say *precisely* what you are estimating. An estimand has two parts: a **unit-specific quantity** and a **target population** (Lundberg et al. 2021). State it outside any model.

**TODO – complete the estimand statement:**

> Unit-specific quantity: the change in \[\_\_\_\_\] for a one-point difference in \[\_\_\_\_\]. Target population: \[\_\_\_\_\].

*(A defensible filling: the change in mean cosmopolitan framing within a country-year, for a one-percentage-point difference in that country's unemployment rate; across EU member states, 2004–2013.)*

Now the identification assumptions. `R/dag_starter.R` builds the graph with `dagify()`, where every arrow is an ordinary R formula written the way you read a regression, effect on the left of the tilde and cause on the right. `framing ~ unemployment` is therefore the arrow unemployment → framing. The causal path and the two confounder pairs are switched on; the arguable arrows sit in the same call behind a `#`, each with a line of justification above it. Open the file, take the `#` off any arrow you believe, re-source, and re-run `adjustmentSets()`. A node joins the picture only once some arrow mentions it, so what you see is the graph you have committed to.

```{r}
#| label: dag
#| fig-cap: "The starter DAG: unemployment → framing, with country and year as confounders."
#| fig-height: 5
source("R/dag_starter.R")
plot_dag(dag)
```

```{r}
#| label: adjustment-set
# What must we adjust for to identify the unemployment -> framing effect?
dagitty::adjustmentSets(dag, exposure = "unemployment", outcome = "framing")
```

The starter graph returns `{ country, year }` – exactly what the two-way fixed effects you fit in Task 3 absorb: country fixed effects adjust for `country`, year fixed effects adjust for `year`. The DAG and the model encode the same identification claim.

**TODO – answer two questions in a sentence each:**

1.  What do **country** and **year** fixed effects adjust for, in plain terms? *(country-constant traits, and shocks common to all countries in a year)*
2.  What can they **not** fix? *(a time-varying, country-level confounder – e.g. GDP growth moving both unemployment and framing within a country over time)*

Whatever set is returned by your DAG becomes field 4 of the preregistration you write in Task 5.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

::: {.callout-note title="Task 3 – Reproduce the recorded result"}
This is the **reproducibility** check. Fit the two-way fixed-effects model that the Multi100 Task-2 constraints point to: cosmopolitan framing on grand-mean-centred unemployment, with country and year fixed effects. The target is **t = −3.804** (df = 233, N = 270) – the value on record for analyst C6HJR in the Multi100 dataset.

```{r}
#| label: fit-corrected
# Grand-mean centre unemployment, exactly as the submitted analysis did. With
# two-way fixed effects this shifts the intercept, not the slope or the t – it
# is the transformation that the constrained specification names, so do it
# explicitly.
euframes <- euframes |> mutate(unemp_c = unemp - mean(unemp, na.rm = TRUE))

# fixest::feols – the bar separates the regression from the fixed effects.
m1 <- feols(mcosmo ~ unemp_c | cntry + year, data = euframes)

tidy(m1)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-corrected
#| tbl-cap: "The constrained model on EUframes_cy.csv."
modelsummary(
  list("two-way FE (fixest)" = m1),
  estimate  = "{estimate}",
  statistic = "t = {statistic}",
  gof_map   = c("nobs", "r.squared"),
  coef_rename = c("unemp_c" = "Unemployment (centred)")
)
```

The coefficient is **−0.00347** with **t = −3.804** – exactly the value recorded for analyst C6HJR, reproduced from the published data and the published model. `feols` reports classical (IID) standard errors by default when two fixed-effect dimensions are present, which is why it matches the `plm` value that the analyst used to three decimals.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Everyone gets the same number, and the five analysts still disagreed"}
You reproduced the recorded value exactly, and so did everyone else in the room, because everyone ran the same code on the same file – which is why reproducibility is the cheap R.

The five Multi100 analysts each wrote their own code for the same claim, and came back with five different answers, one of them not significant. Their pipelines are competent, well-organised work, so the spread is not a quality problem. It is what happens when a claim stated in words leaves several genuinely defensible quantities on the table, and different analysts estimate different ones without noticing they have chosen.

Task 2 named the quantity you are after and drew the graph that your adjustment set follows from. Task 4 now shows you how far the answer moves when the other choices move.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

::: {.callout-note title="Task 4 – Work the menu"}
This task is **exploration, and it is meant to be**. Try several specifications, see what each one does, and get a feel for which choices move the estimate and which barely touch it. Nothing here commits you to anything; that is Task 5.

`try_spec()` takes one argument per axis of the fourteen-axis specification menu, and every argument already carries the baseline you just reproduced – so changing one thing means changing one argument, and everything you do not name stays at baseline. Every call is a real fit: the Level 1 arguments change the question, the Level 2 arguments select which version of the country-year panel is fitted (how the outcome was built from the items, what was done with respondents who mentioned nothing, which published series carries the predictor), and the Level 3 arguments fix the arithmetic. The one exception is the two imputed no-opinion options, whose pooled results are read from a shipped file because they need the respondent-level data that cannot travel; the printout says so when it happens.

**TODO:** run the six calls below, then write your own. Three or four of your own is plenty.
:::

```{r}
#| label: try-baseline
try_spec()                          # the baseline itself
```

```{r}
#| label: try-one-at-a-time
try_spec(outcome   = "mpos")         # all positive framings, not cosmopolitan alone
try_spec(estimator = "pooled_cl")    # no between-country comparison absorbed
try_spec(sample    = "no_bailout")   # drop the assistance-programme countries
try_spec(weights   = "pop")          # let each country count by its adult population
try_spec(noop      = "drop")         # leave out the respondents who mentioned no frame
try_spec(measure   = "es_2064_pop")  # a Eurostat unemployment series instead of the World Bank one
```

Everything you try is logged. Print the log to see the small multiverse you have just built – only the axes you actually varied are shown, so the contrast is readable:

```{r}
#| label: my-experiments
my_experiments()
```

When you have tried three or four, decide which one you would defend if you had to, run it once more so it is the most recent, and submit it. It lands on the live class chart as an **exploratory** result:

```{r}
#| label: submit-exploration
#| eval: false
submit_exploration()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why label it 'exploratory'?"}
Because that is what it is, and the label costs nothing. You chose this specification after seeing what several of them do, so it cannot carry the guarantee that a declared choice carries – it might have been chosen *because* of its result, and neither you nor anyone else can now rule that out.

Almost no published paper tells you which of its analyses were explored and which were planned. Today's chart does, because the room submits twice: once here, and once in Task 5 after declaring, so the two sets of dots can be read against each other.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

::: {.callout-note title="Task 5 – My preregistration"}
The point of preregistration is that you commit to a choice **before** you see what it does. It stops you quietly picking the specification that happens to give the answer you wanted. Here the commitment is real in a mechanical sense too: the choices you declare in the cell below are remembered by the session, and every later cell reads them from here – the model builder refuses code that deviates from them.

Make one choice on each of the fourteen axes of the specification menu, then run the cell. The six Level 1 choices fix the question you are asking; the five Level 2 choices fix how that question is measured; the three Level 3 choices fix the arithmetic. Every axis is live. `claim_align <- TRUE` is the day's convention, applied automatically: negative framings are reverse-coded (1 − y) and the claim-expected sign for growth is flipped, so 'supports the claim' reads as a negative sign for everyone.

Task 2 of Multi100 fixed unemployment as the measure on a gaussian scale; this menu opens both. That is not a stretch beyond the project – Task 1 of Multi100 already shows three of the five analysts reaching for GDP-growth measures when the choice was theirs.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="How this block maps to a real preregistration"}
*A real preregistration, shortened. Each numbered comment maps to a question in the OSF "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org" (the eight-question short form). Because you are reanalysing data that already exist, field 2 also stands in for the prior-knowledge section of the secondary-data template (van den Akker et al. 2021) – the part that AsPredicted leaves out.*
:::

```{r}
#| label: prereg
# ============================================================================
# MY PREREGISTRATION – one specification, declared before seeing its result
# ============================================================================
# 1. The claim I am testing: .................................................
# 2. The data + what I already know: EUframes_cy.csv (270 country-years,
#    public); I know the constrained baseline gives t = -3.804.
# 3. My one specification – one choice on each axis:

# Level 1 – Estimands (each of these changes what is being estimated)
my_outcome      <- "mcosmo"       # mcosmo | mutil | mpos    (positive framings)
                                  # mcomm  | mlib  | mneg    (negative framings)
my_predictor    <- "unemp"        # unemp | growth    (the claim-carrying measure)
my_copredictor  <- "none"         # none | other      (the other macro measure, adjusted for)
my_estimator    <- "fe_twoway"    # fe_twoway | fe_country | re | pooled_cl
my_sample       <- "all"          # all | y2004_2008 | y2009_2013 | no_bailout | no_GR_ES
my_weights      <- "none"         # none | n_cell | n_eff | pop   (re is never weighted)
my_construction <- "share"        # share | count | rate   (share of own mentions, count of the
                                  #   set's items, or count per item in the set)

# Level 2 – Measurement (the same question, put to the data differently)
my_noop         <- "zero"         # zero | drop | split | mi_mice | mi_amelia
                                  #   (respondents who mentioned no frame at all)
my_item_set     <- "all"          # all | un   (with or without the "unemployment" item)
my_cell_weight  <- "unweighted"   # unweighted | design   (cells as interviewed, or design-weighted)
my_measure      <- "wb_nat"       # unemp:  wb_nat | es_1574_act | es_2064_pop | es_2564_lfs | es_1574_tips
                                  # growth: wb_growth | es_growth

# Level 3 – Estimation (the same question and measures, another fit)
my_pred_form    <- "raw"          # raw | log   (growth: raw only; centring or z-scaling
                                  #              would leave t, r and p unchanged)
my_family       <- "gaussian"     # gaussian | beta   (logit link on the cell means; beta
                                  #                    reports z; canonical measurement only)
my_se           <- "conventional" # conventional | clustered   (clustered by country)

claim_align     <- TRUE           # the course convention, applied automatically

# 4. Why these controls, in one DAG-grounded sentence: .......................
# 5. Supported if the claim-aligned coefficient is negative and p < .05;
#    undermined if non-significant or positive. I will report what I get.

prereg()   # checks every choice against the menu and records the declaration
```

An optional mirror form may be used to log preregistrations for the room – the link is shared in the session. It is not required: the cell above, rendered into this report, is your official preregistration.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

::: {.callout-note title="Task 5, continued – build, run and report"}
This is the **robustness** check, and it is the part that your classmates cannot copy from you: together the room samples the multiverse of defensible analyses. You have declared your specification; now translate it into model syntax yourself.

Fill the outcome, the right-hand side, and the estimator code exactly as you preregistered them. `build_model()` knows your declaration and will not accept anything else; its error messages tell you what is off. Write the log form as `log(unemp)`, and add any co-predictor with `+`. You do **not** write the fixed-effects, clustering, or family syntax here – the estimator and family codes stand for it, and `run_spec()` expands them into the real fit.
:::

```{r}
#| label: build-model
my_model <- build_model(mcosmo ~ unemp, estimator = "fe_twoway")
```

When the model is accepted, run it. `run_spec()` fits your preregistered specification for real – the estimator, family, sample and weights expand into the matching `fixest`, `plm`, `betareg` or `glmmTMB` call, and the measurement choices select the version of the panel it is fitted on – and prints its claim-aligned result:

```{r}
#| label: run-spec
run_spec(my_model)
```

Read the output like an analyst: the coefficient and its claim-aligned partial *r* (below zero supports the claim). The five Multi100 analysts run from about the 16th percentile of the specification curve (the most strongly claim-supporting) to about the 68th (near the null); your result is about to join theirs on the class chart.

Now send it to the room. There is nothing to fill in and nothing to transcribe – `report_result()` refits your declared specification, builds the spec label, and always submits on the claim-aligned scale that the chart is drawn on. It prints your submission line and a pre-filled form link; open it and press **Send**. Your dot joins the live [Multiverse](https://codemoreh.github.io/applied-replication/results.html) chart within seconds, this time labelled **declared** rather than exploratory.

```{r}
#| label: report
report_result()
```

If the form will not open on your machine, read the printed numbers to the facilitator and your dot still lands.

**A second declared specification?** Edit the preregistration cell, rerun `prereg()`, rebuild, rerun. The mechanics allow it, and the label does not change – so be clear with yourself about what the second one is. Your first declaration was made without knowing its result. Anything after it was not, which puts it back in the same category as Task 4, and you should say so when you report it.

You did the whole analysis in a plain folder, with no version control and nothing to sign in to. Putting your own work under version control and publishing the rendered report to a live URL is the natural next step – a git and GitHub self-study module walks it click by click on the course site: [Git and GitHub self-study](https://codemoreh.github.io/applied-replication/companion/git-github.html). ::: {.callout-note title="Going further (optional)"}
Time to spare? Each of these is a real fit you can run in this workspace.

- **Sweep a whole axis.** `for (e in c("fe_twoway", "fe_country", "re", "pooled_cl")) try_spec(estimator = e)` fits all four estimators in one go, and `my_experiments()` then prints them side by side. The same trick works for any axis on the menu.

- **The mirror-image expectation.** The claim is about *positive* framing. Preregister a **negative** dimension instead (`mneg`, or communitarian `mcomm`): if poor economic performance lowers positive framing, does it *raise* negative framing? With `claim_align <- TRUE` the reverse-coding (1 − y) is applied for you, so the result restates itself on the same scale as the rest of the curve.

- **Beyond unemployment.** Preregister `my_predictor <- "growth"` (GDP growth, the claim carrier for three of the five original analysts): the claim now expects a *positive* growth coefficient on the positive framings, and the sign convention flips once more automatically. The growth mirror of the Task-3 specification, C6HJR's published Multi100 specification, (`mpos ~ growth + unemp`, two-way FE) gives b = +0.00167, t = 1.59 – non-significant.

- **The full SCORE dossier.** OA's paper went through all three Rs in the SCORE programme and got three different verdicts: its push-button reproduction **failed** (the author-provided Stata code referenced file names that did not match what was available), its reproduction from the source data was recorded as **not reproduced**, and its preregistered secondary-data replication returned a **sign flip** (a positive coefficient, b = 0.002, p = .046, in the opposite direction to the original). Explore reproduction, robustness, and replication side by side at <https://osf.io/h7432/>.
:::
